# Summary of data sources

This section summarizes the paper chosen for this project and where the data is located.

### Chosen Paper

The paper selected for this project is *Utilization of multiple microbial tools to evaluate efficacy of restoration strategies to improve recreational water quality at a Lake Michigan Beach (Racine, WI)* by Kinzelman *et al* (2020). The study uses Illumina 16S rRNA gene sequencing in the methods to analyze microbial communities from environmental samples. I chose this paper because it is related to my research field in recreational water quality and it uses other methods such as microbial source tracking which I also use.

### Hypothesis

The expected results from this re-analysis are that there are significant differences between the taxonomy found at each location. It is also expected that sites with similar characteristics will have similar taxonomy and alpha diversity metrics.

### NCBI SRA

The sequencing data from the paper is located under BioProject [PRJNA640667](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/?term=(PRJNA640667)%20AND%20bioproject_sra%5Bfilter%5D%20NOT%20bioproject_gap%5Bfilter%5D) and accession numbers SAMN15327323- SAMN15327376 for the samples.

### How the data is reported

The sequencing files were uploaded as merged reads when they are actually 2 × 250 paired end reads on a MiSeq Illumina. This caused my pre-processing to treat the samples as single-end reads.

# Summary of re-analysis plan

### Original analysis

The original paper utilizes the following methods for their analysis,

**Pre-processing**

-   QIIME (version 1.9.1) to analyze the 16S rRNA sequencing data
-   clustered the data into OTUs
-   Greengenes dataset (version 13_5) for taxa assignment
-   Rarified the dataset

**Statistical analysis**

Alpha diversity

-   Shannon (non-parametric *t*-tests with 999 permutations)
-   Chaol
-   Simpson
-   PD whole tree

Beta diversity

-   Weighted and un-weighted unifrac

-   Non-phylogenetic distances (Jaccard and Bray Curtis)

-   999 permutations of PERMANOVA and PERMDISP

Differential analysis

-   LEfSe

### Plan for re-analysis

For my re-analysis, I proposed to run the data on DADA2 to get ASVs and perform taxa assignment using the SILVA dataset. This is because ASVs produce higher resolution results to get better taxa assignments. I chose the SILVA dataset instead of Greengenes because it is more up to date and better for bacterial assignment. For statistical analysis, I proposed to use Shannon index for an alpha diversity metric and CLR transformed data and euclidean distances to visualize beta diversity with a PCoA. I plan to reproduce some visuals from the original paper to compare the results with the differing analysis.

**Pre-processing**

-   DADA2 to get ASVs

-   Taxonomic assignment using SILVA (version 138.2)

**Statistical Analysis**

Alpha Diversity

-   Shannon (non-parametric *t*-tests with 999 permutations)

Beta Diversity

-   PCoA with euclidean distances of CLR transformed data

Differential Analysis

-   MaAsLin3

### Feedback from Updated Proposal

After submitting my updated proposal, it was recommended that I also perform a PERMANOVA and differential abundance analysis. The original paper used LEfSe which has a high false positive rate so I plan on usng MaAsLin3 for my analysis.

### Feedback from presentation

The main objective of this re-analysis was to determine differences/similarities in microbial community compositions between locations sampled from the Kinzelman *et al.* paper. My analysis showed that the IEB Overflow had the highest range of alpha diversity which was also seen in the analysis from the paper but the Shannon Diversity calculated in the paper was a lot higher than my values. ## DADA2

### Assign path for fastq files

```{r}
path <- "/Users/jennakraemer/Courses-MB588_BIT588-jkraeme/final_project/fastq" 
list.files(path) # Check files in path
```

This lists the fastq files. Normally it would be separated into forward and reverse reads but since the SRA files are single-end reads, they are all together.

```{r}
fnFs <- sort(list.files(path, pattern = ".fastq", full.names = TRUE))
```

### Identify primers

The paper uses V3-V4 region primers (343-forward TAC GGR AGG CAG CAG and 804-reverse CTA CCR GGG TAT CTA ATC C).

```{r}
FWD <- "TACGGRAGGCAGCAG"
REV <- "CTACCRGGGTATCTAATCC" 

allOrients <- function(primer) {
    # Create all orientations of the input sequence
    require(Biostrings)
    dna <- DNAString(primer)  # The Biostrings works w/ DNAString objects rather than character vectors
    orients <- c(Forward = dna, Complement = Biostrings::complement(dna), Reverse = Biostrings::reverse(dna),
        RevComp = Biostrings::reverseComplement(dna))
    return(sapply(orients, toString))  # Convert back to character vector
}
FWD.orients <- allOrients(FWD)
REV.orients <- allOrients(REV)
FWD.orients
```

### Prefiltering

```{r}
fnFs.filtN <- file.path(path, "filtN", basename(fnFs)) # Put N-filtered files in filtN/ subdirectory
filterAndTrim(fnFs, fnFs.filtN, maxN = 0, multithread = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Count how many reads contain the primer sequence
primerHits <- function(primer, fn) {
  nhits <- vcountPattern(primer, sread(readFastq(fn)), fixed = FALSE)
  return(sum(nhits > 0))
}

# Run primer detection on all orientations of your forward primer
rbind(FWD.Reads = sapply(FWD.orients, primerHits, fn = fnFs.filtN[[1]]),
      REV.Reads = sapply(REV.orients, primerHits, fn = fnFs.filtN[[1]]))

```

### Cutadapt to trim primers

```{r}
cutadapt <- "/opt/anaconda3/envs/cutadapt/bin/cutadapt" 
system2(cutadapt, args = "--version") # Run shell commands from R
```

```{r, message = F}
# Define output directory
path.cut <- file.path(path, "cutadapt")
if (!dir.exists(path.cut)) dir.create(path.cut)

# Input and output file paths
fnFs.cut <- file.path(path.cut, basename(fnFs))

# Reverse complements for completeness
FWD.RC <- dada2:::rc(FWD)
REV.RC <- dada2:::rc(REV)

# Cutadapt trimming flags for single-end reads:
# -g = 5' (forward) primer
# -a = 3' (reverse complement of reverse primer)
R1.flags <- c("-g", FWD, "-a", REV.RC)

# Run cutadapt over each FASTQ file
for (i in seq_along(fnFs)) {
  system2(cutadapt,
          args = c(R1.flags,
                   "-n", 2,                # remove both primers if both present
                   "-o", fnFs.cut[i],      # output file
                   fnFs.filtN[i]))         # input file
}

```

### Checking that primer sequences were removed

```{r}
rbind(FWD.ForwardReads = sapply(FWD.orients, primerHits, fn = fnFs.cut[[1]]), 
      REV.ForwardReads = sapply(REV.orients, primerHits, fn = fnFs.cut[[1]]))
```

```{r}
# Forward and reverse fastq filenames have the format:
cutFs <- sort(list.files(path.cut, pattern = ".fastq", full.names = TRUE))

# Extract sample names, assuming filenames have format:
get.sample.name <- function(fname) tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(fname))
sample.names <- unname(sapply(cutFs, get.sample.name))
head(sample.names)
```

### Checking quality

```{r}
plotQualityProfile(cutFs[1:2])
```

### Filter and Trim Reads

```{r}
filtFs <- file.path(path.cut, "filtered", basename(cutFs))

out <- filterAndTrim(
  cutFs, filtFs,
  maxN = 0,
  maxEE = 2,         # single value, not c(1,2) because single reads
  truncQ = 1,
  minLen = 50,
  rm.phix = TRUE,
  compress = TRUE,
  multithread = TRUE
)
head(out)

```

### Learning error rates

```{r}
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread = TRUE)
```

**Sanity check for estimated error rates**

```{r, eval = F}
plotErrors(errF, nominalQ = TRUE)
```

### Sample Inference

```{r, eval = F}
dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err = errF, multithread = TRUE)
```

### Construct Sequence Table

```{r, eval = F}
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(dadaFs)
dim(seqtab)
```

### Remove chimeras

```{r, eval = F}
seqtab.nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab, method="consensus", multithread=TRUE, verbose=TRUE)

table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab.nochim)))
```

**Check number of reads at each step**

```{r, eval = F}
getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))
track <- cbind(out, sapply(dadaFs, getN),
    rowSums(seqtab.nochim))
# If processing a single sample, remove the sapply calls: e.g. replace
# sapply(dadaFs, getN) with getN(dadaFs)
colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample.names
head(track)

track <- as.data.frame(track)

summarize(track, 
          input = sum(input),
          output = sum(nonchim), 
          percent = output/input)
```

88% of raw reads passed filtering.


## Alpha Diversity

### Calculate Shannon Diversity Index

```{r, warning = F}
alpha <- phyloseq::estimate_richness(ps_mumu, split=TRUE, measures=c("Shannon")) 
head(alpha)
```

### Statistical analysis of alpha diversity

The paper did non-parametric t-tests with 999 permutations so I copied that to be able to compare their statistical results with mine in relation to the alpha diversity.

```{r, message = F}
# Reformat SAM data
SAM_data <- read_csv("/Users/jennakraemer/Courses-MB588_BIT588-jkraeme/final_project/SraRunTable.csv")
# Make sample names row names in sample data
SAM_data <- as.data.frame(SAM_data)
rownames(SAM_data) <- SAM_data$Run
SAM_data$Run <- NULL
SAM <- phyloseq::sample_data(SAM_data)
SAM2 <- merge(SAM, alpha, by="row.names", all=TRUE) 
# Factor locations
SAM2$env_local_scale <- as.factor(SAM2$env_local_scale)

# This code was generated by ChatGPT to loop through all pairs of non-parametric t-tests
groups <- levels(SAM2$env_local_scale)
pairs <- combn(groups, 2, simplify = FALSE)

results <- lapply(pairs, function(p) {
  subset_data <- SAM2[SAM2$env_local_scale %in% p, ]
  
  test <- oneway_test(
    Shannon ~ env_local_scale,
    data = subset_data,
    distribution = approximate(nresample = 999)
  )
  
  data.frame(
    group1 = p[1],
    group2 = p[2],
    p_value = pvalue(test)
  )
})

pairwise_df <- do.call(rbind, results)
pairwise_df$padj <- p.adjust(pairwise_df$p_value, method = "fdr")
pairwise_df
```

### Visualize Shannon over Location

```{r}
# Chat GPT was used to troubleshoot some of the errors I came across with this code chunk and adding letters to the graph
# Get unique groups
groups <- unique(c(pairwise_df$group1, pairwise_df$group2))

# Initialize matrix
p_matrix <- matrix(1, nrow = length(groups), ncol = length(groups),
                   dimnames = list(groups, groups))

# Fill in pairwise comparisons
for (i in 1:nrow(pairwise_df)) {
  g1 <- pairwise_df$group1[i]
  g2 <- pairwise_df$group2[i]
  p  <- pairwise_df$padj[i]     #adjusted p-values
  
  p_matrix[g1, g2] <- p
  p_matrix[g2, g1] <- p
}

p_matrix

letters <- multcompLetters(p_matrix)$Letters # Assign letters to variable
letters
# Create dataframe for the letters with their corresponding locations
letters_df <- data.frame(
  env_local_scale = names(letters),
  label = letters
)

stats <- SAM2 %>%
  group_by(env_local_scale) %>% # Group by location
  summarize(maxY = max(Shannon, na.rm = TRUE))
letters_df <- merge(letters_df, stats, by="env_local_scale")

# Box plot with shannon diversity for each location and letters for statistical differences
ggplot(SAM2, aes(x = env_local_scale, y = Shannon)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_text(data = letters_df,
            aes(x = env_local_scale, y = maxY + 0.1, label = label),
            size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Sample Location") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14, angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12), 
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 13), 
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 13))
```

### Paper's Alpha Diversity Figure

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/paper_alpha.png")
```

My alpha diversity results differ from the paper primarily in magnitude of the Shannon index values. The original values ranged from 5-8.5 and mine ranged from 3-6. The number of OTUs was not reported in the paper so I can't compare those to the number of ASVs that I had. Despite the shift in scale, The spread and trends of the locations were consistent. One of the most interesting similarities is that the location with the highest range of Shannon index metrics is IEB Overflow which is the storm water site. This could mean that the storm water site is variable due to other effects such as precipitation or other anthropomorphic disturbances.

The pairwise group patterns between sites were also similar with the original paper. This could be due to the differences in the ranges of each location. The overall range of each location seems to be smaller than the paper's, this could cause the differences in pairwise groupings. The paper does have the Harbor Wall and N1 sites grouped with IEB Overflow and REC where my results only grouped REC with IEB Overflow.

### Checking for over dispersion

**Original PS object**

```{r}
(psadd::plot_mv(ps_mumu, log=TRUE, title = "Raw Mean-Variance Plot"))
```

**CLR transformed PS object**

```{r}
ps_clr <- microbiome::transform(ps_mumu, "clr")

(psadd::plot_mv(ps_clr, log=TRUE, title = "CLR Mean-Variance Plot"))
```

**VST transformed PS object**

```{r, warning = F}
# Convert to DeSeq object
dds <- phyloseq::phyloseq_to_deseq2(ps_mumu, ~1) 

dds <- DESeq2::estimateSizeFactors(dds)

# get dispersion (variance) estimates for the NB model
dds <- DESeq2::estimateDispersions(dds, fitType = "parametric") 

# check the fit - final estimates (blue) should shrink toward fitted estimates (red)
# if many outliers (large blue circles), consider additional QC steps on your data
DESeq2::plotDispEsts(dds)

# get the transformed data
vsd<-DESeq2::getVarianceStabilizedData(dds)

# copy original ps object
ps_vst <- ps_mumu

# replace the original Otu_table with the transformed data
phyloseq::otu_table(ps_vst) <- phyloseq::otu_table(vsd, taxa_are_rows = TRUE)

(psadd::plot_mv(ps_vst, log=TRUE, title = "VST Mean-Variance Plot"))
```

**Log10 transformed PS Object**

```{r}
ps_log10 <- microbiome::transform(ps_mumu, "log10")

(psadd::plot_mv(ps_log10, log=TRUE, title = "Log10 Mean-Variance Plot"))
```

### Transformation Decision

After looking at mean-variance plots for raw, CLR, VST, and log10 tranformed data, the log10 transformed data looks the most stable. I moved forward with that transformation with euclidean distance for the PCoA. 

### Run ordination via phyloseq::ordinate with option PCoA

```{r}
ps_ord <- phyloseq::ordinate(ps_log10, method = "PCoA", distance = "euclidean")

phyloseq::plot_scree(ps_ord)
```

### Plot ordination results

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = F}
phyloseq::plot_ordination(ps_log10, ps_ord, 
                          type="samples", 
                          color="env_local_scale", 
                          title="PCoA Log10 transformed Euclidean Samples") + 
                          geom_line() + 
                          geom_point(size=5) +
                          labs(color = "Location") +
                          theme_bw()
```

### Paper's Beta Diversity Figure

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/paper_beta.jpg")
```

The paper used a 3D PCoA with weighted Unifrac metrics while I did a PCoA with euclidean distances of log10 transformed ASVs. The groupings of the two figures are very similar. IEB Overflow has a distinct grouping in both PCoAs along with the two river locations overlapping (REC and RR Mouth). The surface waters closer to the lake all overlap as well (N1, N3, and Harbor Wall).

## PERMANOVA with RRPP

### Prep data

```{r, message = F}
# get distance matrix
asv <- read_csv("/Users/jennakraemer/Courses-MB588_BIT588-jkraeme/final_project/asv_table.csv")
asv <- as.data.frame(asv)
rownames(asv) <- asv$...1
asv$...1 <- NULL
# Make the rownames match
rownames(asv) <- sub("\\.fastq", "", rownames(asv))

# Get distance matrix for asv table
asv_d <- vegan::vegdist(asv, method="euclidean")

# ANOVA with distance matrix and locations
anova(vegan::betadisper(asv_d, SAM$env_local_scale))
```
Homogeneity of dispersion was met so I moved forward with RRPP. 

### Run RRPP

```{r, warning = F}
otu.rrpp <- RRPP::lm.rrpp(asv_d ~ env_local_scale,
                   data = SAM, SS.type="III", 
                   print.progress = FALSE, 
                   seed="random", 
                   iter=999) # reduce if needed to run in class

anova(otu.rrpp, effect.type = "F", 
      error = c("Residuals"))
```

The PERMANOVA with RRPP showed a significant difference between locations which was the same result as the authors reported. Sample location explains 55.2% of the variation in community composition.

## Differential Abundance

### Maaslin3

```{r, message=F, eval = F}
# Remove error causing columns
SAM$ReleaseDate <- NULL
SAM$create_date <- NULL
SAM_data$env_local_scale <- as.factor(SAM_data$env_local_scale)
SAM_data$env_local_scale <- relevel(SAM_data$env_local_scale, ref = "IEB_Overflow")


# get distance matrix
asv <- read_csv("/Users/jennakraemer/Courses-MB588_BIT588-jkraeme/final_project/asv_table.csv")
asv <- as.data.frame(asv)
rownames(asv) <- asv$...1
asv$...1 <- NULL
#Rename column headers
asv_table <- asv 
new_names <- paste0("ASV", seq_len(ncol(asv_table)))
colnames(asv_table) <- new_names

# Make the rownames match
rownames(asv_table) <- sub("\\.fastq$", "", rownames(asv_table))

maasfit <- maaslin3::maaslin3(input_data=asv_table, 
                           input_metadata=SAM_data, 
                           output="maasout", 
                           #formula = "~ Treatment + (1|Plot)",
                           #normalization="TSS",
                           #transform="LOG",
                           #standardize=TRUE, # metadata
                           fixed_effects="env_local_scale",
                           #random_effects="Plot",
                           max_significance = 0.00001, #FDR
                           correction = "BH",
                           min_prevalence=0.1,
                           #min_abundance=0
                           )

sigout  <- data.table::fread("./maasout/significant_results.tsv")
head(sigout)
```

### Visualize output

```{r}
# Import maaslin3 table
res <- read.table("maasout/all_results.tsv", 
                  sep = "\t", header = TRUE)

tax <- as.data.frame(phyloseq::tax_table(ps_mumu))  # taxonomy table
tax$feature <- rownames(tax)            

# This is to create taxonomy labels for the figure that are similar to the figures LEfSe figure
# ChatGPT was used to help write the code to create the labels
res_tax <- res %>%
  left_join(tax, by = c("feature" = "feature")) %>%
  mutate(
    lowest = case_when(
      !is.na(Genus)  ~ Genus,
      !is.na(Family) ~ Family,
      !is.na(Order)  ~ Order,
      !is.na(Class)  ~ Class,
      TRUE ~ feature
    ),
    Taxon = paste(Class, lowest, sep = ".")
  )

res_tax <- res_tax %>% mutate(Taxon = make.unique(Taxon))

sig <- res_tax %>%
  filter(qval_individual < 0.00000001) %>%   # VERY important — sig must be rebuilt!
  arrange(desc(abs(coef))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 40)

sig$Taxon <- factor(sig$Taxon, levels = sig$Taxon)

# Plot to look at significant taxa determined from maaslin3
ggplot(sig, aes(x = coef, y = Taxon, fill = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "MaAsLin3 Significant Associations",
    x = "Effect Size (Coefficient)",
    y = "Taxon",
    fill = "Location", 
    caption = "Reference site was IEB Overflow"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

### LEfSe Figure from Paper

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/paper_lefse.jpg")
```

In the paper, the authors main takeaway from the LEfSe results was that Arcobacter and Flavobacterium were enriched in the IEB overflow samples when compared to the other sites. I ran MaAsLin3 with IEB Overflow as the reference level to see what taxa were significantly different in the other locations. Arcobacter had negative coefficients between -6 and -8 for Harbor Wall, N1, N3, and RR Mouth. This aligns with the results from the paper that IEB Overflow was enriched for Arcobacter but my results reported that Flavobacterium was enriched in the N1, N3, and Harbor Wall samples. Arcobacter is a genus that has potential waterborne pathogens so this implies that the storm water samples could be a source of contamination for the recreational water.

# Discussion

The re-analysis did show some differences in results when compared to the paper. The alpha diversity metrics in the re-analysis were much lower across the board when compared to the alpha diversity in the paper. The paper did not report exactly how they rarified the dataset or how many OTUs they had but the higher alpha diversity measurements could be due to how the data was processed. OTUs can inflate diversity metrics because they do not take into sequencing errors into account. Noise from errors can become characterizes as a new species. Another reason could be because the rarefaction causes evenness to increase artificially because of inflated proportional abundance of rare OTUs, removal of singletons in ASVs, or poor error correction with OTUs causing more OTUs present in samples.

The beta diversity methods yielded similar results with the IEB Overflow samples being clustered far from the other samples, the Root River Mouth and REC samples clustered together, and the N1, N3, and Harbor Wall samples clustering close together. The each "type" of sample clustered with other samples of its type which was directly related to their location. These trends were seen on the PCoA from the paper even though they used weighted UniFrac instead of log10 transformed euclidean distances. This information could be used to explain taxonomic differences in locations and which sites are more similar. The PERMANOVA also yielded the same result that the sites are significantly different from each other, which supports the hypothesis. 

The differential abundance methods yielded somewhat different results. The main takeaway from the authors was that Flavobacterium and Arcobacter were enriched in the IEB Overflow samples but when I ran maaslin3 with IEB Overflow as the reference site, flavobacterium was not enriched in IEB but actually enriched in N1, N3, and Harbor Wall when compared to IEB. I did get a similar result that Arcobacter was enriched. This is very important in this context because the storm water samples are enriched for potential pathogens. The beach and harbor wall surface samples also contain potential fish pathogens that are opportunistic to humans. In relation to recreational water quality, if the beach water is mixing with water from the IEB Overflow, that could lead to public health safety issues.

Overall my analysis of the samples brought higher resolution to the taxonomy found in the samples, better pre-processing, error correction, taxa grouping, and differential abundance methods. Some things to note is that the number of samples used in this study for sequencing was relatively small and more samples should be analyzed to get higher confidence in the results. 16S sequencing can also only get down to genus in most cases which does not particularly help with confidence of the presence of potential pathogens. Shotgun sequencing could be a another method explored for recreational water quality to get species level results, although it has its own drawbacks such as lower sensitivity.
